AI Architecture: 12 Layers Behind Modern AI Applications (2026)

Building an AI application is much more than connecting an LLM to a chatbot.

A production-ready AI system brings together 12 essential layers:

1. Business Problem – Define what AI needs to solve.
2. Data Layer – Collect data from databases, APIs and documents.
3. Data Processing – Clean, parse, chunk and validate data.
4. Embedding Layer – Convert data into vector representations.
5. Knowledge Layer – Store embeddings in vector databases.
6. Retrieval Layer – Find relevant context using semantic, keyword and hybrid search.
7. Prompt Engineering – Guide model behaviour with prompts and guardrails.
8. AI Model Layer – Use LLMs like GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama.
9. Agent Layer – Enable planning, reasoning and multi-step execution.
10. Tool Layer – Connect APIs, databases, browsers and external tools.
11. Output Layer – Generate answers, reports, code and workflows.
12. Monitoring & Feedback – Track quality, cost, latency and reliability.

The key takeaway:

An LLM alone doesn't make a production-ready AI application. The real engineering lies in connecting all these layers reliably.

Prompt, context, harness & loop engineering, clearly explained!

An agent is a while loop with four layers of engineering wrapped around it:

- Prompt engineering
- Context engineering
- Harness engineering
- Loop engineering

Each one wraps the last, and the model sits in the middle, so none of them compete with the others. Instead, they just zoom one level further out.

> Prompt engineering:

This defines the input the model sees on one call, often composed of a role, instructions, examples, and an output format.

The techniques here alter the internal computation and reasoning the model goes through due to the wording it sees:

- Chain-of-thought makes it work in steps before answering
- Few-shot examples define the format and the edge cases
- A JSON schema or XML tags make the output parseable by code
- Self-consistency samples a few chains and takes the majority

> Context engineering:

It's everything the model sees on a turn, not just the prompt. That includes the query, retrieved docs, memory, prior turns, and tool outputs from earlier steps.

The window is finite and fills up fast, so the engineering work is to rank inputs and cut everything that isn't pulling weight.

You do this by:

- Retrieving only the chunks relevant to the query, then reranking them
- Keeping key facts out of the middle, where accuracy drops
- Summarizing old turns, evict stale outputs, push big blobs to files

> Harness engineering:

It's the code around the model that defines the tools, parses the calls, retries on failure, and can route work to sub-agents so one handles retrieval and another handles code.

A verifier then grades the result by running tests, validating a schema, etc.

Prompt and context involve getting one call right. The harness involves everything that has to happen around that call for it to run in a real system.

> Loop engineering:

In the usual setup, you manage the outer loop, i.e, you write a prompt, read the turns the agent runs, write the next prompt, and repeat, while catching failures.

This layer hands that job to the agent itself. It kicks off on a schedule or an event, and runs many turns with no prompt in between.

A loop inherently doesn't know when it's finished. An agent can report that it's done and halt while the tests still fail. So the stop can't be the agent's word, but rather it has to be a real signal, like:

- A turn and token cap to stop stuck runs
- A no-progress detector to catch repeated calls
- A completion check to verify the goal with a separate model or a deterministic test

By this layer, you're operating on the whole run, so the engineering moves from writing each prompt to setting the goal and the stop conditions up front and letting it run.

→ critic: reads the log and marks every mistake and every win
→ teacher: turns each one into a one-line lesson
→ librarian: files the lesson into CLAUDE.md. merges duplicates, never deletes a line

AI agent–enabled coding is quietly becoming the new SDLC.

Software development just had its biggest shift since the GUI.

Planning.
Coding.
Testing.
Deployment.

Agents are starting to handle all of it.

Here’s the shift most engineers haven’t noticed yet 👇

Old model: SDLC

• sequential phases
• human-driven execution
• testing happens after development
• changing requirements break timelines

Everything moves step → by → step.

New model: ADLC (Agent-Driven Lifecycle)

• agents write, refactor, and test code
• multiple tasks run in parallel
• requirements evolve dynamically
• feedback loops happen in real time

Instead of a pipeline…

You get a live development system.

6 major shifts happening right now

1️⃣ Driver
Human execution → Autonomous agents

2️⃣ Planning
Fixed scope → Evolving goals & PRDs

3️⃣ Development Speed
Sequential handoffs → Parallel sub-agents

4️⃣ Testing
Post-development QA → Continuous testing

5️⃣ Adaptability
Mid-cycle chaos → Real-time re-planning

6️⃣ Feedback Loop
End-of-project retros → Live monitoring

Some early signals are already here.

According to agentic coding reports:

• teams at Wiz and CRED doubled execution speed
• large-scale repos are being modified autonomously
• complex implementations completed in hours instead of days

How engineers should adapt

1️⃣ Start with one agent
Automate testing first.

2️⃣ Learn to write clear PRDs
Agents execute exactly what you define.

3️⃣ Introduce parallel sub-agents
Break one large task into smaller workstreams.

4️⃣ Review outcomes, not every line of code

5️⃣ Build live feedback loops
Agents should detect issues before you do.

The future of software development isn’t just faster coding.

It’s agent-driven systems building software.

RAG vs. Graph RAG vs. Agentic RAG, clearly explained!

Standard RAG embeds documents into vectors and retrieves the most similar chunks via similarity search. For direct factual lookups, this works well.

But it breaks down when a query needs to connect facts spread across multiple documents. Similarity search retrieves individual chunks, not the relationships between them.

Graph RAG adds a knowledge graph layer on top.

→ During indexing, an LLM extracts entities and relationships from the documents.

→ During retrieval, the system traverses these connections instead of relying on embedding similarity alone.

This is what enables multi-hop queries.

Say a vector DB stores three facts about internal services:

↳ "The checkout service uses payments API."
↳ "The payments API runs on cluster-3."
↳ "Cluster-3 is scheduled for maintenance on Friday."

Someone asks: "Will the checkout service be affected by Friday's maintenance?"

Vector search can likely retrieve facts 1 and 3 because the query mentions "checkout service" and "Friday maintenance."

But it will miss fact 2, which connects the payments API to cluster-3.

That middle fact sits too far from the query in embedding space. It mentions neither "checkout" nor "maintenance," so it never makes it into the retrieved context.

A knowledge graph connects these as linked entities, and graph traversal finds the full path in one query.

Agentic RAG takes a different approach entirely.

Instead of a fixed retrieval pipeline, an LLM agent decides at query time which tools to invoke, which sources to query, and in what order.

Check the visual below to understand the three architectures thoroughly.

One thing to note here is that these three aren't levels of sophistication that you need to graduate through.

Instead, they solve different query types.

↳ Single-hop factual lookups → standard RAG
↳ Multi-hop relationship queries → Graph RAG
↳ Dynamic multi-source tasks with tool use → Agentic RAG

Once the right architecture is in place, the next leverage point is efficiency.

Most RAG architectures rely heavily on vector search, and that layer can be made 32x more memory-efficient using binary quantization.

RAG vs. Vectorless RAG, clearly explained!

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, embedded, and stored in a vector DB. The query gets embedded too, and the top-k closest chunks go to the LLM.

The problem is that similarity and relevance answer different questions.

For instance, five annual reports from one company can likely follow the same template every year, and only the numbers can change.

So a FY2022 question can lie just as close to an FY2025 chunk, and the LLM might answer from the wrong year.

Cross-references introduce another problem. If a chunk mentions "see Appendix G" but looks nothing like the table in Appendix G, that table will never make it to the top-k.

Vectorless RAG drops the embedding model and the vector DB, and replaces similarity search with LLM reasoning instead.

The preprocessing step parses each document's layout into a ToC tree index. Every node holds a section title, its page range, and a short summary, and the whole tree fits in the LLM's context.

At query time, the LLM gets the query along with the tree. It reads the section titles and summaries and picks the few sections most likely to hold the answer.

For example, for a question about debt, it might pick the "Financial Summary" section and also "Appendix G", because its summary says the debt details are there.

The system then pulls those full sections and checks whether the evidence is enough.

↳ If it is, the LLM answers from the full sections, with page citations.
↳ If not, it goes back to the tree and opens more nodes.

The LLM also sees the chat history. So if you ask about assets and then follow up with "what about liabilities?", it goes back to the same report.

The trade-off is that every query now runs LLM calls over the tree.

Top-k vector search will be cheaper in that same run (although not guaranteed to be as accurate), and the tree only helps when documents have real structure.

So the two suit different data:

↳ Use a tree for long, structured documents like filings, contracts, and manuals.
↳ Stick with a vector DB for lots of short, unrelated text.

"The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training"

LLMs can learn entirely new capabilities by simply deleting less than 0.05% of their pretrained weights, without modifying any of the remaining parameters...?

This new paper proposes Deletion Tuning, which learns a binary mask that determines which weights to remove from the model's feedforward layers. Unlike conventional fine-tuning or LoRA, it doesn't learn new weight values, but instead learns which existing connections to disable.

Across RL, SFT, and distillation, Deletion Tuning matches full fine-tuning at the largest scales tested. 

On a 30B-parameter model, it achieves 58.54% vs 58.43% for full fine-tuning, with an adapter roughly 4,000x smaller. 

It also preserves previous capabilities better, while conventional fine-tuning methods lose up to 5.4% of prior-task accuracy.

The reason this might work is because full fine-tuning tends to preserve the model's main weight structure while making changes outside its dominant components. So selectively deleting a tiny fraction of weights can produce a similar pattern of changes without disturbing the rest of the model.

LLMs break every assumption about regular ML inference.

A traditional ML model (CNN, transformer classifier, XGBoost) produces its output in a single forward pass.

Nothing carries over between requests. The GPU does the same kind of work each time.

LLMs don't work like that.

The output is generated one token at a time, autoregressively, which turns a single request into hundreds of sequential forward passes.

The prefill stage is compute-bound, while decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, and running them together on the same GPU hurts both.

The KV cache grows with conversation length and is shared across requests, so routing is no longer about least-busy servers but about which replica already has the relevant prefix cached.

MoE models add expert parallelism on top of that.

None of this exists in traditional ML serving.

That is why an entirely new stack of optimizations has emerged specifically for LLM inference, spanning compression, attention, KV cache management, batching, decoding, parallelism, and routing.

Stateful vs. Stateless MCP core.

(Anthropic's biggest MCP update)

Let us explain what that means:

Until this release, talking to an MCP server worked like a phone call. Both sides ran an initialize handshake, and the server returned a session id carried on every later request.

That session was a live object inside one specific server process, holding the negotiated state.

Picture a restaurant where the waiter who took the order is the only one who knows what was ordered. Everything works until that waiter goes home.

Because that state lives in one process, a balancer could not spread requests across three MCP server instances. Teams pinned clients with sticky sessions or pushed session state into shared storage, which blocked autoscaling and made a single restart drop every open session.

The latest update deletes all of it. The handshake and the Mcp-Session-Id header are gone, and each request now carries its own protocol version, client identity, and capabilities in a _meta field.

Clients that want the capability list up front can call server/discover, but nothing requires it.

The restaurant works the other way around now. That flips the restaurant around. Every request is a written order slip now, and any waiter can fill it.

So any request can land on any instance behind a plain round-robin balancer, with no shared session store. MCP servers become ordinary HTTP services that run on serverless and edge, and survive restarts.

Removing sessions broke three features, so each got rebuilt.

→ Tools that need to ask the user something mid-call used to push that request down a held-open stream. Now the server returns input_required and the client retries with the answers attached.

→ Method and tool names moved into the Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers, so a gateway or rate limiter can route and meter without parsing the JSON-RPC body.

→ List responses carry ttlMs and cacheScope, so clients cache tool catalogs instead of refetching them on every reconnect.

State did not disappear here, it moved somewhere the model can see it.

Applications that need continuity get an explicit handle from a tool and have the model pass it back as an argument on the next call.

A session id in a header is invisible to the model, while a handle in the arguments is something it can read, thread between tools, and recover from after a failed call.

(bookmark this)

Two eval metrics can rank the same two models in opposite orders, and neither one is wrong.

A model that paraphrases the reference can score near zero on BLEU and near the top on BERTScore for the exact same output.

Neither metric is wrong because one is measuring wording and the other is capturing meaning.

This is why LLM evaluation is fragmented into several methods, depicted in the visual below and grouped by what each one assumes:

> Reference-based (ground truth exists):

- BLEU
- ROUGE
- BERTScore

> Judge-based (no ground truth):

- G-Eval
- LLM-as-Judge
- LLM juries

> Human and deterministic:

- Human eval
- DAG

> Built for agents:

- Trajectory accuracy
- Multi-turn eval

> Run as a gate:

- Safety eval

To use them in practice, most of these metrics are already implemented in Opik, which is open source (20k+ stars) and runs them over traced production data. You can start using them in a few lines of code.

GitHub repo: https://t.co/vahjkkfJCt

(don’t forget to star it ⭐️)

That said, metrics only point at the failing case.

The rest of the work is still done manually, like inspecting the trace to see where the span went wrong, editing a prompt or a tool description, re-running, and checking that the fix did not break anything else.

My co-founder wrote a walkthrough (with code) that automates this loop using Opik.

It explains the full lifecycle where a failing trace gets diagnosed, the fix runs against the exact input that failed, and that input stays in the eval set as a regression case so it does not recur.

Read it below.

LLM evaluation is where you find out if your model is actually good, or just sounds good.

A model can write impressive answers and still fail on accuracy, reasoning, consistency, safety, or hallucinations.

That’s why evaluating an LLM goes beyond asking, “Does this answer look good?”

You need to test things like:
• Accuracy
• Relevance
• Reasoning
• Factuality
• Hallucination
• Safety
• Consistency
• Instruction following

And depending on the use case, you might use benchmarks, human evaluation, LLM-as-a-judge, or custom evaluation datasets.

Building an LLM is only half the job. Knowing whether it actually works is the other half.

LLM-as-judge without the trace is a false-alarm machine. On 72 ground-truth cases, a text-only judge matched trace-based judging on recall and fired 5x more false alarms.

A three-phase comparison of evaluation harnesses for enterprise analytics agents (arXiv 2611.14493, Nov 10). Three paradigms, two agents, frozen execution traces: trace-based LLM judging, text-only judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics.

The mechanism is attribution. A trace judge sees every tool call, intermediate result and state change, so when a number is wrong it can point at the step that produced it. A text-only judge sees only the final answer and has to infer the process, so a plausible answer with no visible evidence gets flagged as risky. Same recall, five times the noise a human then triages.

Two more findings:

- Functional testing and security red-teaming had zero overlap in the failures they caught. 24 novel failures surfaced only in the discovery phase. One harness gives false confidence, not coverage.
- 97% of configurations passed the stability threshold, and stability was agent-independent. Repeat-run noise lives in the harness, not in the model.

Caveats: one research setting, two agents, frozen traces, 72 cases, and the authors evaluated their own frameworks.

Takeaway: judge the trace, not the transcript. Then add an adversarial framework for security. Two harnesses, disjoint failure sets.

"Correct Answers from Insufficient Histories: A Controlled Study of Agent Memory Evaluation" — new paper (arXiv preprint, Nov 9, 2026). https://t.co/09pLyRpkI1

In plain terms: agent memory systems hand a model only part of its past history (a trimmed or compressed log), then most evals (automated tests) check the answer against a reference worked out from the FULL history. This paper shows a model can "pass" that check even when the part it was shown could not possibly determine the answer, so a high score can hide lucky guessing.

3 distinct takeaways for product builders:

- A matching answer is not proof the memory worked. With logs cut short so the answer was provably not in view, Qwen3-32B still matched the full-history reference on 87 of 203 cases (DeepSeek-V4-Flash: 85 of 203). Recommendation: in your memory evals, label each test case as "answer is in the context" or "answer is not in the context", and count hits on the second kind as unsupported, not as wins.

- Asking the model to say "I don't know" is not enough. Both prompts explicitly told the model to reply UNDETERMINED when the evidence was missing, yet it gave a concrete answer on 196 of 203 (Qwen) and 182 of 203 (DeepSeek) such cases. Recommendation: if guessing is costly, enforce abstention in code (for example, check whether the retrieved log is complete for the time asked about) instead of relying on the prompt.

- A 99% LLM judge (a model used to grade other models' answers) still slips. The DeepSeek-V4-Flash judge was right on 1,908 of 1,920 constructed cases (99.38%) but twice approved answers the visible log did not support, and two outputs were cut off; a simple rule-based program scored 1,920 of 1,920 with zero model calls. Recommendation: when correctness can be checked by rules, run a deterministic checker first and use the LLM judge only for what rules cannot cover.

Experiment setup (from the paper):
- Environment: synthetic, executable device logs (each report has 8 fields: ids, times, device, action, argument, outcome; duplicates and rejected actions included); 4 query types: count of accepted routes, first route, last route, device state.
- Evidence labels: "insufficient" is proven by building a second legal history that yields byte-identical visible context but a different answer; "sufficient" by public rules (complete-log marker, a complete record after the query cutoff, or first route already visible).
- Readers: hosted Qwen3-32B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, temperature 0, 64-token output limit; 80 confirmation histories, 1,600 requests per reader; context cut to a 768-token budget (a token is roughly a word piece).
- Conditions: raw-text prefix, whole-record prefix, CSV prefix, plus full raw and full CSV controls; the CSV vs raw effect on appropriate answers stayed inconclusive.
- Metrics: reference agreement vs. "context appropriateness" (answer only when the visible log determines it, otherwise abstain); 10,000-replicate bootstrap 95% intervals clustered by history.
- Judge study: 120 held-out histories, 1,920 constructed candidates, compared against finite and extended rule programs and a program-first hybrid.

8 AI model architectures, visually explained:

LLMs get so much attention that it's easy to overlook the rest of the field. Different inputs, tasks, and deployment constraints have led to very different model designs.

Here are eight specialized AI model architectures:

1. LLM (Large language models)

Text is split into tokens, mapped to embeddings, and processed through transformer layers. The model generates its response by predicting successive tokens.

↳ GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

2. LCM (Large concept models)

Moves prediction to the sentence level. Sentences become SONAR embeddings, and the model predicts the next sentence representation. Meta explored both autoregressive and diffusion-based versions.

↳ Meta's LCM research introduced this approach.

3. LAM (Large action models)

Connects a user's request to actions in an environment. These systems interpret intent, plan steps, and use interfaces or tools, often checking results before continuing.

↳ Rabbit R1, Microsoft UFO, Claude Computer Use.

4. MoE (Mixture of experts)

A router assigns token representations to selected expert networks inside the model. Activating a subset of experts adds model capacity without running every expert for every token.

↳ Mixtral, DeepSeek, Switch Transformer.

5. VLM (Vision-language models)

Combines visual representations with language processing. A vision encoder extracts image features, which are connected to a language model so it can answer questions about visual content.

↳ GPT-4V, Gemini, LLaVA.

6. SLM (Small language models)

Uses fewer parameters to reduce memory and compute requirements. These models can run locally, with quantization often reducing their deployment footprint further.

↳ Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B, Llama 3.2 1B.

7. MLM (Masked language models)

Learns by predicting hidden tokens using context on both sides. This bidirectional training produces representations useful for retrieval, classification, and other language-understanding tasks.

↳ BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa.

8. SAM (Segment Anything Model)

An image encoder processes the image, while a prompt encoder handles points, boxes, or masks. A mask decoder combines them to identify the requested regions.

↳ Meta's SAM supports interactive segmentation and image annotation.

These aren't eight mutually exclusive categories. A small model can process images, and a language model can use MoE layers. Some labels describe architecture, while others describe training or intended use.

There's another approach I kept outside the image because it alters how a model handles context rather than introducing a separate model family.

Recursive language models, from MIT, put the input into a Python environment that a root model can inspect through code.

The model can search or slice that input, then make recursive model calls on selected portions instead of loading everything into its own context window.

The reported experiments handled inputs beyond 10 million tokens without retraining, with gains over the base model even on some tasks whose inputs already fit its context window.

Every behavioural evaluation rests on an assumption borrowed from experimental design: that the subject behaves the same whether or not it knows it's being watched. 

In human research that assumption fails often enough to have a name & the standard remedies like blinding & deception work precisely because the subject can't tell the difference.

In the last post, we learned how Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) allows AI agents to retrieve relevant information from external knowledge before generating responses. Today, we'll explore the technology that makes semantic search possible—embeddings and vector databases.

Embeddings and Vector Databases – FAISS, ChromaDB, and Pinecone

Traditional databases search using exact keywords. AI agents, however, need to understand the meaning behind text, even when different words are used. This is made possible through embeddings and vector databases.

What Are Embeddings?

Embeddings are numerical vector representations of text generated by AI models.

Instead of storing words as plain text, embeddings capture their semantic meaning.

For example, the sentences:

→ "How do I deploy a Docker container?"

→ "How can I run my application using Docker?"

have different wording but similar meanings, so their embeddings will be close together in vector space.

This allows AI systems to perform semantic search rather than simple keyword matching.

What Is a Vector Database?

A vector database stores embeddings and retrieves the most semantically similar vectors for a given query.

When a user asks a question, the workflow is:

→ Convert the question into an embedding

→ Search the vector database

→ Retrieve the most similar document chunks

→ Pass the retrieved context to the LLM

→ Generate an informed response

This retrieval process is the foundation of modern RAG applications.

FAISS

FAISS (Facebook AI Similarity Search) is an open-source library developed by Meta for efficient similarity search.

Features include:

→ Extremely fast vector search

→ Optimized for large datasets

→ Runs locally

→ Supports millions of embeddings

FAISS is ideal for high-performance local AI applications.

ChromaDB

ChromaDB is an open-source vector database designed specifically for AI applications.

Benefits include:

→ Simple Python integration

→ Persistent storage

→ Metadata filtering

→ Ideal for RAG prototypes

It is one of the easiest vector databases to use when building AI agents.

Pinecone

Pinecone is a fully managed cloud vector database.

It provides:

→ Automatic indexing

→ High availability

→ Horizontal scalability

→ Low-latency semantic search

→ Managed infrastructure

Pinecone is well suited for production AI systems that require scalable vector search without managing servers.

Choosing the Right Vector Database

→ FAISS for fast local similarity search

→ ChromaDB for lightweight RAG applications and development

→ Pinecone for cloud-native, production-scale deployments

The choice depends on your application's scale, infrastructure, and deployment requirements.

🔎 Search text, images and video frames with one encoder, then use the same model to choose between predefined answers.

MetaEncoder v1 from Meta combines multimodal retrieval and closed-set decisions in a roughly 28.4B-parameter model using the Muse Glimmer architecture.

Its interface has three main operations:

▪️ encode: turn content into an embedding for storage, clustering or comparison.
▪️ retrieve: rank a collection against a query.
▪️ decide: answer predefined questions about a state, with scores and probabilities.

🧩 Each embedding is a normalized 6,656-dimensional vector. An input can contain text, images, video frames or a mixture of them.

Instructions tell the model what the representation is for. A document and a search query can use different instructions, and the same image can produce different embeddings depending on the task.

For video, the wrapper accepts a list of frames. If you supply more than eight, it uniformly subsamples them to eight.

You can also encode a corpus once and reuse its vectors for repeated searches. The wrapper returns float32 embeddings and cosine-similarity rankings; it does not build a compressed vector database for you.

⚖️ The interesting part is decide. Give it a scenario and questions such as “Is this a shopping request?” or “Which category fits this image?” It embeds the question and candidate answers, compares their similarity, and selects an option.

Supported outputs include yes/no, a choice among 2–26 options, and a score over ordered labels.

Probabilities come from a softmax over similarity scores, using the contrastive training temperature of 0.02. The included calibration method can fit that temperature to labeled examples from your own task. A sharply peaked distribution describes the model’s preference among those options, rather than proving the answer correct.

🛠️ The release includes downloadable weights and a Python wrapper. It requires transformers 5.15 or newer, and the model card says one 80 GB GPU holds the model in bf16.

For document search, media tagging and routing, the practical appeal is reusing one representation model across retrieval and structured decisions. There is no generated explanation to parse: the output is the selected value and its associated scores.

here are some points you should know about embeddings beyond just using them as vectors for search.

mteb is not one test. it measures retrieval, classification, clustering, reranking, pair classification, semantic similarity, and summarization. a model can be strong overall while still being weak at search.

embeddinggemma reaches 69.67 on MTEB english v2 at 768 dimensions, despite having only about 300M parameters and this shows smaller models can be surprisingly competitive.

qwen3-embedding scales from 0.6B to 8B parameters, with published english v2 scores from 70.70 to 75.22. bigger models improve, but not always in proportion to their size. 

vector size changes storage cost. embeddingGemma supports 768, 512, 256, and 128 dimensions. smaller vectors save storage, but quality gradually declines. 

moe is entering embedding models. nomic embed v2 stores 475M parameters but activates about 305M during inference, using eight experts and top-2 routing. 

more experts do not automatically mean lower latency. routing tokens between experts creates communication and scheduling overhead so efficiency depends on how well the hardware and software handle that routing.

beir tests retrieval across 18 datasets and nine information-retrieval tasks, including fact checking, medical search, duplicate questions, entity search, and scientific retrieval. so 1 retrieval score is never the whole story. 

benchmark averages can hide the real result. a model may improve sharply on domains represented in its training data and barely improve elsewhere. serious evaluations should report per-task scores, domain splits, model size, instructions, and data provenance.

so understand the next phase of embedding research is not simply “make the model bigger.”

but better data; better teacher supervision; better task coverage; better evaluation; and better quality per parameter.

VECTOR DATABASES FOR LLMs
PINECONE, WEAVIATE, & PGVECTOR FOR SEMANTIC SEARCH

Modern LLM applications rely heavily on vector databases to enable semantic search, retrieval, & Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Traditional databases search using exact keywords.
Vector databases search using meaning.

WHAT IS A VECTOR DATABASE?

→ A vector database stores embeddings instead of plain text
→ Embeddings are numerical representations of meaning
→ Similar meanings are placed close together in vector space
→ This enables semantic similarity search

Instead of matching exact words, vector databases answer:

→ Which documents mean something similar to this query?
→ Which chunks are contextually related?

WHY VECTOR DATABASES ARE ESSENTIAL FOR LLMs

LLMs do not automatically remember your private data.

Vector databases allow you to:

→ Store embeddings of documents
→ Perform fast similarity search
→ Retrieve relevant context
→ Inject retrieved data into prompts
→ Reduce hallucinations

They are the backbone of:

→ RAG systems
→ AI chatbots
→ Enterprise knowledge assistants
→ Semantic search engines

CORE VECTOR DATABASE SOLUTIONS

1) PINECONE

→ Fully managed vector database
→ Designed specifically for high-scale semantic search
→ Cloud-native and production-ready

KEY FEATURES

→ Real-time similarity search
→ Automatic scaling
→ Metadata filtering
→ High availability

BEST FOR

→ Production LLM applications
→ Large-scale SaaS AI systems
→ Teams that want managed infrastructure

ADVANTAGE

→ No infrastructure management required
→ Optimized performance out of the box

2) WEAVIATE

→ Open-source vector database
→ Hybrid search (vector + keyword search)
→ Built-in modules for AI integrations

KEY FEATURES

→ GraphQL-based queries
→ Hybrid BM25 + vector search
→ Built-in classification and modules
→ Cloud and self-hosted options

BEST FOR

→ Customizable AI systems
→ Research projects
→ Applications requiring hybrid search

ADVANTAGE

→ Flexible and extensible
→ Strong community support

3) PGVECTOR

→ Extension for PostgreSQL
→ Adds vector similarity search to Postgres
→ Combines relational and vector capabilities

KEY FEATURES

→ Cosine similarity and inner product search
→ Works inside existing PostgreSQL database
→ Simple integration with backend systems

BEST FOR

→ Applications already using PostgreSQL
→ Small to medium LLM systems
→ Teams wanting unified storage

ADVANTAGE

→ No separate vector database required
→ Structured + semantic search in one place

HOW VECTOR DATABASES ENABLE SEMANTIC SEARCH

Step-by-step workflow:

→ Documents are chunked
→ Each chunk is converted into embeddings
→ Embeddings are stored in the vector database
→ User query is converted into an embedding
→ Similar vectors are retrieved
→ Retrieved context is injected into the LLM prompt
→ LLM generates grounded response

COMPARISON SUMMARY

PINECONE

→ Fully managed
→ High scalability
→ Enterprise-ready

WEAVIATE

→ Open-source
→ Hybrid search support
→ Highly customizable

PGVECTOR

→ PostgreSQL extension
→ Unified database architecture
→ Simpler infrastructure

CHOOSING THE RIGHT VECTOR DATABASE

Choose Pinecone if:

→ You want managed infrastructure
→ You are building large-scale SaaS

Choose Weaviate if:

→ You want flexibility and hybrid search
→ You prefer open-source control

Choose pgvector if:

→ You already use PostgreSQL
→ You want relational + vector data together

wtf is an agent harness.

An agent is a model plus a harness.

Model reads the context and picks the next action. The harness is all the code that turns that choice into work.

Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity, OpenClaw and Hermes Agent are all harnesses.

8 common parts every agent harness shares:

1. The loop
• Sends the context to the model and runs whatever tools it asks for
• Feeds the results back in for the next step
• Decides when the task is finished

2. Tools and sandbox
• Give the model a terminal, files, a browser and your connected apps
• Run every task inside its own isolated computer
• Keep the damage from a bad command inside the sandbox

3. Subagents
• Take side tasks off the main agent and run them in parallel
• Start each one with a fresh context window
• Send back only a short summary, so the main context stays clean

4. Context management
• Decides what the model sees on every turn
• Loads skills and files only when the task needs them
• Summarizes old history before the context window fills up

5. Memory
• Stores progress notes, git history and skills on disk
• Lets a new session read what the last one did
• Picks the work up where it stopped

Cybersecurity and AI Security are closely related, but they focus on different aspects of protecting digital systems.

Cybersecurity focuses on protecting computers, networks, applications, databases, and digital infrastructure from attacks.

It protects the systems we build, the data we store, and the networks we use.

For example, a cybersecurity team might defend a web application against SQL injection, phishing, ransomware, and unauthorized access.

AI Security focuses on protecting AI systems, models, training data, inference pipelines, and AI-powered applications from attacks and misuse.

It addresses threats that emerge when machine learning models and AI capabilities become part of software systems.

For example, an AI security engineer might protect an LLM application against prompt injection, data poisoning, model extraction, and sensitive information leakage.

The key difference?

Cybersecurity protects digital infrastructure and information.

AI Security protects AI systems and their entire lifecycle, while also addressing the risks AI introduces into existing applications.

Cybersecurity focuses on:

↳ Network security and firewalls.
↳ Identity and access management (IAM).
↳ Application and API security.
↳ Cloud and infrastructure security.
↳ Endpoint protection.
↳ Encryption and data protection.
↳ Vulnerability management.
↳ Incident response and threat detection.

AI Security focuses on:

↳ Prompt injection and jailbreak attacks.
↳ Training data poisoning.
↳ Model theft and model extraction.
↳ Adversarial machine learning.
↳ LLM data leakage.
↳ RAG and vector database security.
↳ AI agent and tool-use security.
↳ Model supply chain security.
↳ AI red teaming and evaluation.

Imagine building an AI-powered SaaS application.

Traditional cybersecurity protects:

- User authentication and authorization.
- APIs and databases.
- Cloud infrastructure.
- Network traffic and application endpoints.

AI Security protects:

- The LLM against prompt injection.
- RAG pipelines against malicious documents.
- AI agents against unauthorized tool execution.
- Models against data poisoning and extraction.
- AI outputs against unsafe or manipulated behavior.

You need both to build secure AI-powered applications.

Cybersecurity provides the broader security foundation, while AI Security addresses threats specific to AI systems and AI-enabled workflows.

AI Agents 101: 𝗔𝗜 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗠𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆.

In general, the memory for an agent is something that we provide via context in the prompt passed to LLM that helps the agent to better plan and react given past interactions or data not immediately available.

It is useful to group the memory into four types:

𝟭. Episodic - This type of memory contains past interactions and actions performed by the agent. After an action is taken, the application controlling the agent would store the action in some kind of persistent storage so that it can be retrieved later if needed. A good example would be using a vector Database to store semantic meaning of the interactions.

𝟮. Semantic - Any external information that is available to the agent and any knowledge the agent should have about itself. You can think of this as a context similar to one used in RAG applications. It can be internal knowledge only available to the agent or a grounding context to isolate part of the internet scale data for more accurate answers.

𝟯. Procedural - This is systemic information like the structure of the System Prompt, available tools, guardrails etc. It will usually be stored in Git, Prompt and Tool Registries.

𝟰. Occasionally, the agent application would pull information from long-term memory and store it locally if it is needed for the task at hand.

𝟱. All of the information pulled together from the long-term or stored in local memory is called short-term or working memory. Compiling all of it into a prompt will produce the prompt to be passed to the LLM and it will provide further actions to be taken by the system.

We usually label 1. - 3. as Long-Term memory and 5. as Short-Term memory.

9 techniques to generate better LLM outputs:

An instruction alone, with no examples, schema, or stated constraints, is the default way to generate an LLM response.

This is zero-shot prompting, and it serves as the baseline. But when outputs aren't good enough, the first thing you should try is to improve the prompt, not a model upgrade.

There are 8 prompting techniques that you can use:

- Few-shot prompting: Show the model a few input-output examples. It picks up the pattern and applies it to new inputs.

- Chain-of-thought (CoT): Ask for step-by-step reasoning. Breaks complex problems into smaller, verifiable steps.

- Prompt hierarchy: Use system, developer, and user prompts at different authority levels. Higher levels override lower ones.

- Role-specific prompting: Assign a persona like "You are a security researcher." The model conditions on a different slice of its training data.

- Negative prompting: Specify what the LLM should NOT do. "Do not use marketing language" works as a hard constraint.

- JSON prompting: Define a JSON schema in the prompt. The LLM returns structured output matching that schema.

- Attentive reasoning queries (ARQ): Replace free-form CoT with structured, domain-specific questions. In testing, it hit 90.2% instruction adherence vs. 81.5% for direct prompting.

- Verbalized sampling: Explicitly prompt the LLM to generate multiple responses with probability scores. Recovers the output diversity that RLHF alignment suppresses.

They stack well together. Few-shot + CoT. JSON + Negative prompting. ARQ is essentially a structured version of CoT for agentic conversations.

Of course, better outputs will also come from better context, tool access, and retrieval.

But these 9 techniques live entirely in the prompt and involve working with the same model, infrastructure, and setup. You are just structuring the prompt differently to get better outputs from an LLM.

Once the prompt is doing its job, the next lever is how much compute the model spends before it answers.

We covered that separately, walking through chain of thought, best-of-N, self-refinement, and tree search, and why each of them only keeps paying off when you have a reliable way to verify the output.

Jev-style scoring vs. LLM decoding vs. structured output, clearly explained:

Many LLM requests do not need newly written text.

Routing, classification, policy checks, and ranking usually already have a known set of valid answers, and the only question is which answer best matches the input.

Consider a support ticket:

"I was charged twice for the same subscription."

The application must route it to either billing, technical support, or account access.

With normal LLM decoding, the model goes through a full reasoning process. A decoding rule selects one token, appends it to the sequence, and runs the model again.

This continues until the model responds with something like:

"Based on the customer's query, this ticket should go to billing."

The application then has to parse that text to recover the decision it needed from the beginning.

Structured output handles this better, but the underlying process is still generation.

A grammar or schema masks illegal next tokens at every step. The model cannot produce arbitrary prose, but it still generates/decodes the full JSON token by token:

"""
{
  "team": "billing"
}
"""

This is useful when the application needs unknown values, nested fields, or tool arguments. The schema guarantees the shape of the response.

Jev-style scoring handles fixed-choice decisions differently.

The application provides the query, the input state, and the allowed answers before inference.

This time, instead of decoding a sentence or JSON object, the model scores the predefined candidates:

"""
billing → 0.90
technical support → 0.10
account access → 0.00
"""

The application receives the selected label and its probability distribution directly.

The applicability entirely depends on the downstream use case. They expose different output contracts and perform different types of inference work.

- LLM decoding is ideal when the application needs newly written text. It can also return a label, but it must generate and parse that label like any other response.

- Structured output decoding is ideal when the values are not known beforehand, but the application requires a predictable schema. The model still generates the response token by token while the decoder prevents invalid structures.

- Jev-style scoring is ideal when the valid answers are already known. It cannot write an explanation or produce an unknown field value. Instead, it compares the supplied candidates and returns their probabilities without decoding a sentence or JSON object.

50 terms every AI builder should know:

1.) LLM: a large language model trained to predict the next word

2.) Token: a small chunk of text the model reads and writes

3.) Context window: how much text the model can see at once

4.) Prompt: the instruction you give the model

5.) System prompt: hidden instructions that shape every response

6.) Temperature: how random or creative the output is

7.) Inference: running a trained model to get an answer

8.) Latency: how long you wait for a response

9.) Hallucination: when the model confidently makes things up

10.) Fine-tuning: training a model further on your own data

11.) RAG: fetching relevant documents and feeding them to the model

12.) Embedding: turning text into numbers that capture meaning

13.) Vector database: storage built to search embeddings fast

14.) Chunking: splitting documents into pieces for RAG

15.) Reranking: sorting search results so the best ones go first

16.) Agent: a model that plans and takes actions on its own

17.) Tool calling: letting the model use APIs, code or search

18.) MCP: a standard way to connect models to tools and data

19.) Agent loop: think, act, observe, repeat

20.) Subagent: a smaller agent handed one piece of the job

21.) Orchestration: coordinating multiple agents or steps

22.) Memory: what an agent remembers between sessions

23.) Guardrails: rules that block unsafe or off-topic output

24.) Prompt injection: hidden text that tricks a model into misbehaving

25.) Jailbreak: a prompt that gets around a model's safety rules

26.) Evals: tests that measure how well your AI performs

27.) Benchmark: a standard test used to compare models

28.) LLM-as-judge: using one model to grade another's output

29.) Ground truth: the correct answer you test against

30.) Structured output: forcing the model to reply in JSON or a set format

31.) Function schema: the definition of a tool the model can call

32.) Streaming: showing the response word by word as it's generated

33.) Caching: reusing past results to save time and money

34.) Prompt caching: reusing a repeated prompt prefix to cut cost

35.) Rate limit: how many requests you're allowed per minute

36.) Open weights: a model you can download and run yourself

37.) Distillation: training a small model to copy a big one

38.) Quantization: shrinking a model so it runs faster and cheaper

39.) LoRA: a cheap way to fine-tune only a small part of a model

40.) GPU: the chip that runs AI models

41.) Multimodal: a model that handles text, images, audio or video

42.) Reasoning model: a model that thinks step by step before answering

43.) Chain of thought: the model writing out its reasoning first

44.) Few-shot: giving the model examples in the prompt

If you’re self-hosting an LLM, you will hit this choice sooner or later.

vLLM or SGLang?

Both are open source. Both batch requests on the fly, cache memory, and give you an OpenAI-style API. On paper they look almost the same. The difference is in what each one cares about most.

vLLM started with PagedAttention. It splits the model’s memory into small blocks and places them anywhere on the GPU, so very little space goes to waste. Over time it has grown into the safe, broad choice: lots of models, lots of hardware, many LoRA adapters, and the biggest community.

SGLang started with RadixAttention. It keeps past requests in a tree. When a new request shares the same start, like the same system prompt or the same chat history, it reuses that work and only computes what is new. That makes a real difference for chat apps, agents, and RAG, where many requests begin the same way.

So my simple rule:

Lots of repeated prompts and multi-step flows? Try SGLang. Need wide model and hardware support with less friction? Start with vLLM.

And please don’t pick based on someone else’s benchmark chart. Both take one command to start. Run your own traffic through both and look at your own numbers.

The idea is pretty simple.

You define the exact decisions you want the evaluator to make, Jev evaluates each one and returns probabilities, and DeepEval uses those results to calculate the final score.

For example, with an AI agent you can evaluate the trace itself, checking whether the agent selected the right tools, followed the expected sequence of actions, and actually completed the task.

Jev handles those semantic judgments, while the scoring logic stays outside the model.

That is the main difference from a normal LLM-as-a-judge setup.

With a generative judge, the model often has to interpret the rubric, reason about the response, and generate the evaluation itself.

With JevEval, you define the decision structure upfront.

You can also assign different weights to different checks or use `strict_mode` when every requirement needs to pass.

So if one part of the agent workflow matters more than another, you can reflect that directly in the scoring logic instead of leaving the entire evaluation to the judge model.

Key capabilities:

- Evaluate agent outputs and traces with Jev
- Define custom checks as bounded decisions
- Use yes/no, score, and closed-choice questions
- Weight different checks or require all of them to pass
- Evaluate both single-turn outputs and multi-turn conversations

This is where Jev makes a lot of sense for evals.

If you already know what needs to be checked, you can define those decisions upfront, let Jev handle the semantic judgment, and keep the final scoring deterministic.

- Strands Evals, LLM judge with the full OpenTelemetry trace: F1 0.896, false positive rate 10.3%
- PromptFoo, text-only judge plus red-team: F1 0.716, FPR 48.7%
- Agenta, deterministic regex: F1 0.629, FPR 100%

What separates them is what they can see. On SQL correctness, where query text can be injected into any harness, both LLM judges hit 89% recall. On tool correctness, which needs the execution trajectory, the trace judge gets 89% and PromptFoo 11%. On groundedness the trace judge has 0% FPR, PromptFoo 52%, because text-only sees tool result metadata instead of the data itself.

Two things I did not expect. Decision consistency across 5 repetitions: 82% trace judge, 92% PromptFoo, 100% regex, and one Qwen3 config flips 4 of 5 verdicts. An LLM judge is fine for finding failure patterns, not for gating CI/CD. And 9 of 72 human labels were wrong: valid SQL with the wrong partition filter, a calibration coefficient read backwards.

Red-teaming is not a substitute. 24 novel failures, zero overlap: the trace judge found functional bugs, PromptFoo found schema metadata leakage and prompt disclosure. Run both.

Most LLM-powered evals are BROKEN!

These evals can easily mislead you to believe that one model is better than the other, primarily due to the way they are set up.

G-Eval is one popular example.

Here's the core problem with LLM eval techniques and a better alternative to them:

Typical evals like G-Eval assume you’re scoring one output at a time in isolation, without understanding the alternative.

So when prompt A scores 0.72 and prompt B scores 0.74, you still don’t know which one’s actually better.

This is unlike scoring, say, classical ML models, where metrics like accuracy, F1, or RMSE give a clear and objective measure of performance.

There’s no room for subjectivity, and the results are grounded in hard numbers, not opinions.

LLM Arena-as-a-Judge is a new technique that addresses this issue with LLM evals.

In a gist, instead of assigning scores, you just run A vs. B comparisons and pick the better output.

Just like G-Eeval, you can define what “better” means (e.g., more helpful, more concise, more polite), and use any LLM to act as the judge.

LLM Arena-as-a-Judge is actually implemented in @deepeval (open-source with 12k stars), and you can use it in just three steps:

- Create an ArenaTestCase, with a list of “contestants” and their respective LLM interactions.

- Next, define your criteria for comparison using the Arena G-Eval metric, which incorporates the G-Eval algorithm for a comparison use case.

- Finally, run the evaluation and print the scores.

This gives you an accurate head-to-head comparison.

Note that LLM Arena-as-a-Judge can either be referenceless (like shown in the snippet below) or reference-based. If needed, you can specify an expected output as well for the given input test case and specify that in the evaluation parameters.

It's 100% open-source with 12k+ stars and implements everything you need to define metrics, create test cases, and run evals like:

- component-level evals
- multi-turn evals
- LLM Arena-as-a-judge, etc.

Moreover, tracing LLM apps is as simple as adding one Python decorator.

If you're building AI systems, learn these 15 things:

1. Error analysis before metrics: Study real production failures, identify recurring patterns, and build metrics around actual problems.

2. Golden datasets: Build versioned test datasets with expected outputs, rubrics, edge cases, and different levels of difficulty.

3. Synthetic data generation: Generate test cases across personas, intents, complexity levels, and edge cases instead of creating hundreds of similar questions.

4. Deterministic assertions: Validate JSON schemas, required fields, regex patterns, SQL queries, and code execution before using an LLM judge.

5. RAG evaluation: Measure retrieval quality using Recall@K, MRR, and nDCG. Evaluate answer faithfulness separately.

6. Agent trajectory evaluation: Track every tool call, argument, result, and reasoning step. Measure whether the agent takes the right path, not just whether it reaches the right answer.

7. pass@k vs. pass^k: Understand the difference between succeeding at least once and succeeding consistently across multiple runs.

8. Multi-turn evaluation: Simulate users with hidden goals, constraints, and changing requirements to uncover memory and state-management failures.

9. LLM judge calibration: Compare model-generated evaluations against human-labelled examples. Measure false positives, false negatives, and judge accuracy.

10. Pairwise evaluation bias: Account for position bias and verbosity bias when comparing two model outputs.

11. Statistical significance: Learn confidence intervals, bootstrapping, and paired testing. A small improvement in your eval score doesn't automatically mean your model got better.

12. Evaluation in CI/CD: Run regression tests whenever prompts, models, tools, or retrieval configurations change.

13. Online evaluations: Monitor production traffic, run asynchronous evaluations, and use shadow deployments to compare new models without affecting users.

14. Cost and latency evaluation: Track tokens, cost per successful task, and p50/p95 latency alongside answer quality.

15. Continuous feedback loops: Convert every meaningful production failure into a new test case. Your evaluation dataset should improve with every release.

A model can look impressive in a demo and still fail miserably in production.

Don't just measure whether your AI gives good answers.

Measure whether it gives reliable answers, consistently, at an acceptable cost and latency.

Your models will change. Your prompts will change. Your evaluation infrastructure should keep getting better.

Top 12 agentic use cases for Jev:

(bookmark this)

Jev handles semantic decisions that ordinary code cannot express reliably. It returns typed answers and probabilities, while code continues to cover the workflow.

Here are 12 practical use cases for Jev:

1. Browser next action

> Convert the current DOM state into a bounded action such as click, type, or stop. Code executes only valid operation-target pairs. There are already several open-source Jev web agents.

2. Context compaction

> Decide which events from a long agent trace should remain. The selected text stays verbatim instead of being replaced with a generated summary.

3. Skill and context loading

> Compare the current user turn against the available skills. Load only the instructions needed for that turn instead of filling the context window with every skill.

4. Typed tool-call compilation

> Map a natural-language request to a function and fill its typed arguments. Each argument is evaluated separately before code allows execution.

5. Citation verification

> Check whether a quoted passage exists and whether the surrounding evidence supports the claim. The output can be supported, unsupported, or contradicted.

6. Extraction verification

> Run a cheap extractor first, then use Jev to verify questionable fields. Clean records stay on the fast path while uncertain ones reach a reasoning model.

7. Agent trace evaluation

> Turn raw trajectories into queryable labels such as progress and repetition. This avoids asking another LLM to write a full review of every run.

8. Semantic regression tests

> Replay a trace suite against a new agent build. Semantic checks can then pass or block prompt, model, tool, and policy changes in CI.

9. Jevgrep code search

> Search a codebase by what the code does rather than its exact words. Jev scores candidate snippets and returns the most relevant code first.

10. Entity alignment

> Compare two candidate records and decide whether to merge, review, or keep them separate. Candidate generation remains deterministic while Jev handles semantic identity.

11. Retrieval reranking

> Let embeddings retrieve a broad candidate set, then use Jev to reorder passages by relevance. The generation model receives the most useful evidence first.

12. Memory promotion gate

> Capture a completed agent trace, then judge whether its corrections contain a reusable lesson. Trace-backed lessons can be promoted while task-specific noise is discarded.

Two classic ways to a smarter AI: a bigger model or more training data. The third is test-time compute: let it think longer on each question. For some problems, a small model given time can beat a big one answering instantly.

Google DeepMind researchers showed how adaptive test-time compute can outperform simply scaling model size

essential for AI engineers building reasoning systems that need to decide where additional inference compute actually matters

fixed compute strategies waste budget because different prompts benefit from different scaling methods

the paper studies two primary mechanisms for scaling test-time computation:

1. Process-Based Search
explores multiple solution paths and uses dense process reward models to score intermediate reasoning steps

2. Adaptive Response Updating
updates the model's response distribution based on the specific prompt and its difficulty

3. Compute-Optimal Allocation
dynamically assigns test-time compute per prompt instead of applying the same inference strategy everywhere

prompt difficulty → adaptive compute allocation → search or response updating → verified solution

the compute-optimal strategy improves test-time compute efficiency by more than 4x compared to a best-of-N baseline

on suitable tasks, a smaller model with additional test-time compute can even outperform a model 14x larger in FLOPs-matched evaluations

turning compute allocation into an adaptive engineering layer makes Test-Time Compute Engineering a direct alternative to scaling model parameters

New UC Santa Barbara paper shows that LLM math discovery can skip test-time training, since an evolving memory scored better and used far less compute.

i.e. evolving memory beats test-time training on math discovery, with far less compute.

Test-time training lets a model improve during a search by running RL on its own scored attempts. Those weight updates are slow and costly, so the method is hard to scale to bigger models.

They built TTME, which keeps the weights fixed and stores lessons in memory. The memory holds practical coding rules from earlier tries and the ideas behind score gains, which guide later attempts.

Across 5 math tasks, 2 frameworks, and 3 models, TTME beat the reported test-time training scores every time. With Qwen3-8B on 3 tasks, it used 82.8% to 84.6% fewer FLOPs and 47.7% to 58.4% less runtime than test-time training.

If your LLM search loop has an automatic checker, try a memory of lessons before paying for weight updates mid-search.

“Test-Time Scaling Makes Overtraining Compute-Optimal”

Most scaling laws assume you train once and answer once.

But this paper says that if you already know you’ll spend extra compute at test time by sampling many answers, then you should train a different model.

So instead of a bigger model trained the usual way, it can be better to train a smaller model for much longer.

As smaller models are cheaper to sample many times, those extra tries can beat one expensive shot from a larger model.

So the real thing to optimize is not just training compute, but training + inference together. And this paper shows overtraining can actually become the compute-optimal choice.
